title: Clopen partitions on a w-local affine scheme
statement:
The patch topology of an affine scheme is compact Hausdorff. For a w-local
[def-weil-pbc-w-local] affine scheme $X$, its closed point set $X^c$ is a
profinite space, and restriction identifies clopen partitions of $X$ with
clopen partitions of $X^c$. An open subset containing a part of $X^c$
contains the corresponding components of $X$.

proof.text: Write $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-qcqs-scheme-spectral] to the affine scheme $X$: the required quasi-compactness and quasi-separatedness follow from [lem-weil-pbc-affine-scheme-qcqs], whose Mathlib matches are AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.compactSpace_of_isAffine (Mathlib/AlgebraicGeometry/AffineScheme.lean:561) and AlgebraicGeometry.quasiSeparatedSpace_of_isAffine (Mathlib/AlgebraicGeometry/Morphisms/QuasiSeparated.lean:167). Thus $X$ is spectral. By [lem-weil-pbc-spec-localization-away-basic-open], the $D(f)$ form an open basis and each is homeomorphic to $\operatorname{Spec}(A_f)$. This affine spectrum is quasi-compact by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-scheme-qcqs], so every $D(f)$ is quasi-compact. Every quasi-compact open is a finite union of these basis opens: cover it by basis opens contained in it and take a finite subcover. Thus the topology generated by all quasi-compact opens and their complements equals that generated by the $D(f)$ and $V(f)$, namely the patch topology of [def-weil-pbc-w-local]. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-spectral-constructible-topology-quasi-compact] and [lem-weil-pbc-spectral-constructible-topology-hausdorff] to obtain compactness and Hausdorffness of that topology.

source.place: Proof, first paragraph; Topology Tag 0901 (lemma-constructible-hausdorff-quasi-compact) supplies the two cited patch properties

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-proper-ideal-contained-in-maximal], every prime $\mathfrak p$ is contained in a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$. In the Zariski topology of [def-weil-affine-spectrum], $\overline{\{\mathfrak p\}}=V(\mathfrak p)$: each closed zero locus containing $\mathfrak p$ contains all primes containing it, and $V(\mathfrak p)$ is such a closed locus. In particular $\mathfrak p$ specializes to $\mathfrak m$, and a point is closed exactly when its prime is maximal. The closure of a point is connected: every nonempty relatively open subset of that closure contains the point, since its complement is relatively closed, so two nonempty disjoint relatively open subsets cannot cover it. Consequently $\mathfrak p$ and $\mathfrak m$ belong to the same connected component. For w-local $X$, the unique closed point of that component, supplied by [def-weil-pbc-w-local], must therefore be $\mathfrak m$. Every point of that component specializes to this same closed point.

source.place: Proof, second paragraph, last two sentences; Algebra Tag 00E0 (lemma-Zariski-topology) supplies maximal-ideal existence

proof.text: The w-local condition [def-weil-pbc-w-local] says that $X^c$ is Zariski closed, hence $X^c=V(J)$ for an ideal $J\subseteq A$. By [lem-weil-pbc-spec-quotient-homeomorphism-zero-locus], $\operatorname{Spec}(A/J)$ is homeomorphic to $X^c$. All its points are closed: each corresponds to a closed singleton of $X$, which remains closed in the subspace. By the closed-point/maximal-prime criterion proved in step 2, now for the ring $A/J$, every prime of $A/J$ is maximal. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-zero-dimensional-spectrum-profinite] to $A/J$. It follows that $X^c$, with its Zariski subspace topology, is compact Hausdorff and totally disconnected.

source.place: Proof, third paragraph, first three sentences; Algebra Tags 00E5 (lemma-spec-closed) and 04MG (lemma-ring-with-only-minimal-primes)

proof.text: By the spectrality established in step 1 and [def-weil-spectral-space], $X$ satisfies every hypothesis of [lem-weil-pbc-quasicompact-components-clopen-intersection]. Hence each connected component is the intersection of the clopen neighbourhoods of any of its points. Two distinct points $c,d\in X^c$ are in distinct components by the uniqueness clause of [def-weil-pbc-w-local]. Since $d$ is outside the component of $c$, some Zariski clopen $U\subseteq X$ contains $c$ but not $d$.

source.place: Proof, second paragraph (component fact) and third paragraph (separation of distinct closed points); Topology Tag 005F, lemma-connected-component-intersection

proof.text: Let $E\subseteq X^c$ be clopen and put $F=X^c\setminus E$. Both are compact, being closed in the compact space from step 3. For a fixed $c\in E$ and each $d\in F$, step 4 gives a clopen $U_{c,d}\subseteq X$ containing $c$ and excluding $d$. The sets $F\cap(X\setminus U_{c,d})$ are relatively open and cover $F$, so finitely many suffice. Their corresponding finite intersection $U_c$ contains $c$ and misses $F$. If $F$ is empty use $U_c=X$. Now the relatively open sets $E\cap U_c$ cover $E$, so finitely many suffice again. The union $U$ of the corresponding finitely many $U_c$ is Zariski clopen and satisfies $U\cap X^c=E$. If $E$ is empty use $U=\varnothing$. This writes out both finite-cover arguments of the blueprint; it uses only steps 3 and 4.

source.place: Proof, third paragraph: compactness first separates each point of E from its complement, and then covers E

proof.text: Every nonempty clopen $W\subseteq X$ contains a closed point: choose $x\in W$ and specialize to the component's closed point by step 2; since $W$ is closed, that specialization stays in $W$. Thus two clopen subsets with the same restriction to $X^c$ coincide, since their symmetric difference is clopen and has no closed point. Together with step 5 this proves the bijection on clopen subsets. Restriction preserves complements, finite unions and intersections. A clopen partition of $X^c$ has finitely many nonempty parts: its open parts cover the compact space of step 3; a finite subcover contains every nonempty part because the parts are disjoint. Lift those finitely many parts by step 5 and lift every empty part to the empty set. These lifts give pairwise disjoint parts covering $X$: any nonempty intersection or nonempty complement of their union would contain a closed point, contradicting the partition on $X^c$. Conversely, any clopen partition of $X$ restricts to one of $X^c$, and the uniqueness just proved recovers every original part. Thus restriction identifies arbitrary clopen partitions, including the empty partition of an empty spectrum. Each lifted part is a union of components, because intersecting a connected component with a clopen and its complement cannot separate it; its components are exactly those whose unique closed point lies in the original part.

source.place: Proof, third paragraph: extension is unique because every nonempty clopen contains a closed point; explicit partition argument

proof.text: Finally let $O\subseteq X$ be Zariski open and contain a part $E\subseteq X^c$. If a connected component has its unique closed point $c$ in $E$, step 2 shows every point $x$ of that component specializes to $c$. Since $c\in O$, also $x\in O$: otherwise the closed complement of $O$ would contain $x$ and its specialization $c$. Thus $O$ contains all the corresponding components, including the clopen part constructed above.
